How often should I water my Venus flytrap?

Rather than watering on a fixed schedule, keep the soil damp at all times and let the weather set the pace. The easiest way is the tray method: stand the pot in about 1 cm of mineral-free water and top the tray up whenever it empties. In a hot summer window that might mean refilling every day or two, while in cool weather it can stretch to a week. The soil should never dry out completely - flytraps are bog plants.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Tap water okay?

No, tap water will slowly kill a Venus flytrap. Almost all tap water carries dissolved calcium, magnesium and other salts, and those minerals accumulate in the soil until they burn the roots. Use distilled, reverse osmosis or rainwater instead, ideally under about 50 ppm TDS.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What exactly is the tray method and how do I set it up?

You sit the potted plant in a shallow saucer or tray and keep roughly 1 cm of mineral-free water in it, letting the mix wick moisture up from below. Any plastic tray, takeaway container or plant saucer works as long as the pot has drainage holes so the water can get in. Refill it when it runs dry rather than letting the pot sit bone dry for days. This is the standard way to grow flytraps through the growing season.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I've been using bottled spring water for a month, is that a problem?

Yes, spring water is a problem - it is bottled precisely because it carries dissolved minerals, often 100 to 400 ppm TDS. A month is not usually fatal, so switch to distilled or rainwater now and flush the pot by pouring a litre or two of clean water slowly through the top until it drains out the bottom. Do that a couple of times over a week and watch for new growth coming in healthy.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I think I killed my flytrap, the leaves are going brown at the edges!

Take a breath, that pattern is usually mineral burn rather than death. Crispy brown edges that creep inward over weeks nearly always mean the water carries dissolved salts, so check what you have been using and swap to distilled, RO or rainwater. Flush the soil with clean water a few times, cut off fully dead leaves, and give it at least 6 hours of direct sun. New traps that come in green tell you the plant has turned the corner.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is a Brita filter good enough for my carnivorous plants?

Unfortunately not. Carbon pitcher filters like Brita are designed to improve taste by removing chlorine and some organics, but they leave dissolved calcium, magnesium and sodium behind almost untouched. Run filtered tap water through a TDS meter and you will typically see nearly the same reading as the tap. You need distilled, reverse osmosis or rainwater, all of which are effectively mineral-free.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
distilled vs reverse osmosis - does it actually matter which one I use?

Both are fine and your plant will not notice the difference. Distilled water is essentially 0 ppm, and a decent RO unit puts out somewhere in the 5 to 30 ppm range, which is comfortably below the 50 ppm ceiling you want. Pick whichever is cheaper and easier for you - store-bought distilled for one or two plants, RO if you have a collection worth the up-front cost.

Can I use rainwater for my Venus flytrap?

Rainwater is arguably the best option and it is free. It is naturally very low in dissolved solids, usually well under 20 ppm, and it is what these plants evolved to receive in the wild. Collect it off a clean surface rather than from an old asphalt roof if you can, and it is worth a quick TDS check the first time to confirm your setup is clean.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How should I collect and store rainwater so it stays usable?

A barrel or a few food-grade jugs under a downspout is plenty for a windowsill collection. Keep the containers covered and out of direct sun so algae and mosquito larvae do not take hold, and screen the inlet to keep out leaves and grit. Stored rainwater keeps for months and a bit of harmless organic sediment does not bother flytraps. If a container ever smells foul, tip it out and start again.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What TDS reading should I be aiming for?

Keep your water under about 50 ppm total dissolved solids, and lower is better. Distilled sits near 0, rainwater usually lands between 5 and 20, and a healthy RO membrane gives you 5 to 30. Anything up around 150 ppm and beyond is typical tap water and will cause visible mineral burn within a season.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do I really need to buy a TDS meter?

You do not strictly need one if you are buying distilled water, since you already know what is in the bottle. A meter becomes genuinely useful if you collect rainwater, run an RO unit, or want to confirm a filter is doing what its packaging claims. They cost very little and they take the guesswork out - just remember the target is under 50 ppm.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What soil mix should I plant a Venus flytrap in?

A 1:1 mix by volume of sphagnum peat moss and perlite is the classic recipe and it is hard to beat. Coarse silica sand can replace the perlite if you prefer a heavier mix, and pure long-fiber sphagnum also grows excellent plants. The non-negotiable part is that the mix must contain no nutrients at all - no fertilizer, no compost, no additives. Rinse the perlite or sand in clean water before mixing to wash off dust and any residual salts.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I just use regular potting soil?

No, potting soil will kill a Venus flytrap, usually within a couple of months. It is loaded with nutrients, lime and often wetting agents, and flytrap roots are adapted to nutrient-poor bog peat and simply burn in it. Repot into a 1:1 sphagnum peat and perlite mix, washing the old soil gently off the roots with mineral-free water.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I bought a bag of Miracle-Gro moisture control mix, will that work?

Do not use it. Anything marketed with feed, moisture control or wetting agents contains added fertilizer and surfactants, both of which are toxic to flytrap roots. Look for plain sphagnum peat moss with nothing on the label except peat, then cut it half and half with rinsed perlite.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is the difference between peat moss and long-fiber sphagnum for flytraps?

Peat moss is decomposed sphagnum sold as a dense brown material, and it is normally mixed 1:1 with perlite to keep it open. Long-fiber sphagnum is the dried whole plant, stringy and airy, and it can be used on its own straight out of the bag. Both are nutrient-free and both grow great flytraps, so it comes down to what you can source and whether you want the extra drainage perlite provides.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do I have to rinse perlite before using it?

Yes, always rinse it. Bagged perlite carries a lot of fine dust and can pick up dissolved salts in storage, and that dust also irritates your lungs when it is dry. Tip it into a sieve or bucket, run mineral-free water through it until the water runs clear, then mix it with your peat. The same goes for silica sand.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I use play sand from the hardware store in my flytrap mix?

Only if it is pure silica sand, and never builder's sand. Builder's and mason's sand is full of lime and other mineral contaminants that will poison the plant. Look for washed silica or horticultural quartz sand with no additives, rinse it thoroughly, and mix it 1:1 with peat if you are using it in place of perlite.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Why does everyone say silica sand specifically?

Because silica is chemically inert - it does not release calcium or other minerals into the soil the way limestone-based sands do. Flytraps live in nutrient-poor, low-mineral bog conditions, so every component of the mix has to be neutral. Rinse the silica sand before use and combine it roughly 1:1 with sphagnum peat moss.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I put a bit of fertilizer in the pot to help it grow?

Never fertilize the soil of a Venus flytrap. Even a weak dose burns the fine roots and the plant can decline within weeks, because it is adapted to soil with essentially no available nutrients. It gets its nitrogen from insects it catches, so a plant in good light outdoors feeds itself. If it is indoors year round you can offer a small dried insect to a trap now and then, but nothing goes into the soil.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is a terracotta pot okay for a flytrap?

Avoid terracotta and any unglazed clay. Porous clay leaches minerals into the soil and also wicks salts up through the walls, which is exactly what you are trying to prevent. Plain plastic pots are the standard choice, and glazed ceramic is fine if the glaze is intact inside and out.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What size pot does a Venus flytrap need?

Give it depth more than width. The roots can run 10 to 13 cm down, so a pot at least 10 cm deep and preferably closer to 15 cm suits an adult plant. A taller pot also holds moisture more evenly and keeps the crown from sitting in the wettest zone. Plastic is best, and make sure it has drainage holes.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Does the pot need drainage holes if I am using the tray method?

It absolutely does. The tray method works by water wicking up through the holes into the mix, so a sealed pot leaves the soil dry on top and stagnant at the bottom. Any plastic nursery pot with holes will do. If you like a decorative glazed container with no holes, use it as a cachepot with the real pot sitting inside it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I water my flytrap during winter dormancy?

Cut back noticeably but do not let it dry out. Take the pot out of the standing tray and simply keep the mix just damp, watering from the top every week or two depending on temperature. Cold, wet and stagnant conditions with no active growth invite rot, so damp rather than saturated is the goal. When growth resumes in spring, go back to the 1 cm tray.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
It is January and my flytrap has stopped growing. Should I keep the tray topped up?

That pause is normal dormancy, not a problem, and it changes how you water. Empty the tray and switch to keeping the soil merely damp, checking it every week or so and adding a little mineral-free water from the top when the surface starts to feel less moist. Standing water plus cold temperatures and no growth is the main way people lose plants over winter. Full tray watering resumes when new leaves appear in spring.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can you overwater a Venus flytrap?

During the growing season it is very hard to overwater one, because these are bog plants that naturally sit in saturated peat. Roughly 1 cm of standing water in a tray is right, but do not submerge the pot so the crown is underwater for long stretches. The real overwatering risk is winter, when a dormant plant kept in a full tray at low temperatures can rot. Underwatering kills far more flytraps than overwatering does.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I went away and the soil dried out completely. Is my plant dead?

Not necessarily - the rhizome underground is tougher than the leaves suggest. Rewet the mix straight away with distilled or rainwater, and if the peat has gone water-repellent, top water it slowly several times until it takes up moisture again, then return it to a 1 cm tray. Leave the shrivelled leaves in place for now and give it a few weeks in good light. If a new leaf pushes up from the centre, the plant is recovering.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What does mineral burn actually look like?

It shows up as browning that starts at leaf tips and trap edges and works inward, leaving dry, crispy margins while the rest of the leaf still looks alive. It is gradual - a slow decline over weeks or months rather than a sudden collapse - and new leaves come in progressively smaller and weaker. You may also see a whitish crust on the soil surface or around the pot rim. The cure is switching to mineral-free water and flushing the pot.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How do I flush mineral buildup out of the soil?

Take the pot out of its tray, set it in the sink, and pour distilled, RO or rainwater slowly through the surface until several pot volumes have drained out the bottom. For a 10 cm pot that is roughly a litre or two per flush. Repeat two or three times over the following week, then discard the runoff and put the plant back in a clean tray. Badly encrusted soil is better replaced entirely with fresh peat and perlite.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Does water temperature matter? I keep my distilled water in the fridge.

Room temperature water is kinder to the plant. Ice-cold water straight from the fridge, roughly 4 C, can shock the roots of a plant that is actively growing in a warm window. Let the jug sit out until it reaches about 18 to 24 C before you use it. In summer, water sitting in a tray in full sun can also get hot enough to cook roots, so shade the tray or top it up with cooler water during heatwaves.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do Venus flytraps need high humidity? Should I get a terrarium?

They do not need high humidity, and this is one of the most common myths about them. As long as the soil is consistently wet, ordinary household humidity of 40 to 50 percent is completely fine. Terrariums usually do more harm than good because they cut the light, and light matters far more - a flytrap needs at least 6 hours of direct sun. Put it on a sunny sill or outdoors and keep the tray topped up.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I mist my flytrap every day?

Misting does very little for a flytrap and is not a substitute for wet soil. Humidity is not the limiting factor for this species, so a daily spray mostly just gets the leaves wet. If you mist, use distilled or rainwater only, since tap water will leave mineral deposits on the leaves. Your effort is better spent keeping about 1 cm of clean water in the tray and giving the plant more sun.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is the difference between a humidity tray and the tray method?

A humidity tray is a pebble-filled saucer that keeps the pot above the waterline so the plant gets evaporation without wet roots - it is aimed at tropical houseplants. Flytraps want the opposite: the pot sits directly in about 1 cm of water so the soil stays saturated. Skip the pebbles and let the pot make contact with the water. The humidity is beside the point for this species.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How should my watering change through the seasons?

In spring and summer, when the plant is growing hard and in full sun, keep a constant 1 cm of water in the tray and expect to refill every one to three days in hot weather. As autumn cools and growth slows, let the tray run lower and refill less frequently. Through winter dormancy, drop the tray altogether and just keep the mix damp, checking weekly. The plant's water demand tracks its growth and the temperature.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Top watering or bottom watering - which is better?

Bottom watering with a tray is the routine method because it keeps moisture even, avoids disturbing the crown, and means you can leave the plant for a couple of days. Top watering is what you use for a specific purpose: flushing salts out of the mix, rewetting peat that has dried hydrophobic, and watering through winter dormancy. If you do top water, pour gently at the soil surface rather than over the traps.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Should I let the tray dry out between waterings?

A short dry spell of a day or so does no harm and can even improve oxygen at the roots, but do not let the soil itself dry out. In practice, refill the tray as soon as you notice it empty rather than deliberately waiting. Peat that dries out fully becomes water-repellent and is a nuisance to rewet. Keeping about 1 cm of water in the tray more or less continuously through the growing season is the simplest approach.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How deep should the water in the tray be exactly?

About 1 cm is the number to remember, or roughly a third of a centimetre to a centimetre and a half depending on how fast your setup dries. That is deep enough to keep the mix saturated by wicking without drowning the crown. Do not stand the pot in half its own depth of water for weeks on end. Deeper trays are only sensible outdoors in extreme summer heat, and even then not during dormancy.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What mix should I use when I repot, and how often?

Repot every 1 to 2 years into fresh 1:1 sphagnum peat and rinsed perlite, or straight long-fiber sphagnum if you prefer. Peat breaks down and compacts over time and slowly accumulates whatever minerals sneak in, so fresh media makes a real difference. Wet the mix with distilled or rainwater before planting rather than after, and set the white bulb of the rhizome just below the surface. Water it in and return it to the tray.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
When in the year is the best time to repot?

Early spring, just as dormancy ends and before the plant puts on its main flush of growth, is ideal. The plant recovers quickly then and roots into the new mix within a few weeks. You can repot in summer if you must, but expect a stall of a week or two afterwards. Avoid repotting in the depths of winter dormancy unless the soil is clearly contaminated.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
We are on well water here, can I use that?

Well water is usually the worst option of all - it tends to be very high in dissolved calcium and magnesium, often 200 to 600 ppm TDS or more. Even occasional use will drive mineral burn. Collect rainwater, buy distilled, or run an RO unit, and check the output with a TDS meter to be sure you are under 50 ppm.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Our house has a water softener. Is softened water safe for flytraps?

Softened water is especially bad for them, worse than the hard water it replaced. A softener does not remove minerals, it swaps calcium and magnesium for sodium, and sodium is directly toxic to carnivorous plants. Never use it, even diluted. Look for an outside tap plumbed before the softener, or simply use distilled or rainwater.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I use the water from my dehumidifier or air conditioner?

Yes, condensate is essentially distilled and typically reads under 10 ppm, which makes it a great free source. The catch is the collection surfaces, which can harbour mould, dust and metal residue, so keep the reservoir and coils clean. Give it a TDS check now and then, and if the water smells bad or looks oily, discard it. Otherwise it is fine to use straight in the tray.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Does boiling tap water make it safe to use?

No - boiling does the opposite. It drives off some chlorine but evaporates pure water and leaves the dissolved minerals behind, so the water that remains is slightly more concentrated than what you started with. Only distillation, which captures the steam, or reverse osmosis actually removes the mineral load. Stick to distilled, RO or rainwater.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
I'm away for two weeks in July. How do I keep my flytrap alive?

Move it to a deeper reservoir before you go: sit the pot in a container with 3 to 5 cm of mineral-free water, which is more than you would normally use but will carry it through the absence. Put it somewhere with good light but out of the very hottest afternoon sun so the reservoir does not overheat or evaporate too fast. A larger, deeper pot buffers longer than a small shallow one. Return it to the usual 1 cm tray when you get back.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Green stuff and little moss patches are growing on my soil surface. Bad sign?

Generally harmless. Algae and moss thrive in constantly wet peat under bright light, and they are a sign your conditions are right rather than wrong. Only step in if the moss is thick enough to smother the crown or bury small traps, in which case peel it back with tweezers. If you also see a white or grey crust rather than green growth, that is mineral deposit and points to your water source.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
There is a white crusty layer on top of my soil and around the pot rim. What is it?

That is mineral deposit left behind as water evaporates, and it means dissolved solids are getting into the pot. Check your water first - tap, spring, filtered or well water are the usual culprits - and switch to distilled, RO or rainwater. Scrape off the crust, then flush the pot with a litre or two of clean water two or three times. If the buildup is heavy, repot into fresh 1:1 peat and perlite instead.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I water my flytrap with the water I siphon out of my fish tank?

No, aquarium water is exactly what you want to avoid. It is full of dissolved nitrates, phosphates and mineral salts from fish waste and feed, which is wonderful for houseplants and toxic for carnivores. Flytraps need nutrient-free water and nutrient-free soil. Use distilled or rainwater and let the plant get its nitrogen from insects.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
At the grocery store there is distilled, purified and drinking water. Which one do I buy?

Buy the one labelled distilled, nothing else. Purified and drinking water are often just filtered or remineralised tap water and can run 50 to 250 ppm TDS. Steam-distilled water is near 0 ppm and is the safe choice. If the only option is labelled reverse osmosis with nothing added, that also works.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Does the peat need to be a special lime-free type?

Yes, look for plain sphagnum peat moss with no lime, fertilizer or wetting agent added. Some horticultural peats are pH-adjusted with lime for vegetables, and that added calcium is harmful to flytraps. The ingredient list should say sphagnum peat moss and nothing more. Flytraps want acidic, nutrient-free media at around pH 4 to 5, which untreated peat provides naturally.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Won't leaving it in standing water give my flytrap root rot?

Not under normal growing-season conditions, because this is a bog plant whose roots are adapted to permanently saturated peat. Root rot becomes a real risk in two situations: standing water during cold winter dormancy, and a pot with no drainage where water goes stagnant. Keep the tray to about 1 cm, use a pot with holes, and empty the tray for the winter. Done that way, constant moisture is exactly what the plant wants.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My flytrap came from the shop in a small pot with moss on top. Should I change anything?

Nursery pots are usually filled with acceptable peat and just topped with decorative sphagnum, so there is no emergency. Peel back the surface moss if it is smothering the traps, sit the pot in about 1 cm of distilled or rainwater, and move it to your sunniest spot for at least 6 hours of direct light. Plan to repot into fresh 1:1 peat and perlite in a deeper plastic pot the following spring. If it arrived in dark, rich-looking soil rather than peat, repot it right away.
